highlights.title: Highlights
highlights.description:
Conway's refinement conjecture [Con76, p. 46] asks for four omnific integers $e,f,g,h$ whenever $ab=cd$, with $a=ef$, $b=gh$, $c=eg$ and $d=fh$. It suffices to split any divisor of a product into a divisor of each factor. Conway normal form turns this into a question about generalised power series with integer constant coefficient.

The series argument starts with the germs of translated truncations. The first germ outside a suitable subalgebra is transcendental over it. This gives two polynomial presentations in characteristic zero. For real exponents the full series ring is polynomial over its finite-support subring, so greatest common divisors split divisors at a single Archimedean class. At a limit of classes the ring of germs of series with small support is polynomial over a field, so divisors split modulo the ideal of series with support bounded away from zero. Restricting to a sufficiently small convex subgroup makes these identities exact. Induction on the classes met by the support combines the two cases. Conway's construction of a number between two small sets supplies the cofinality and completeness needed for surreal exponents.

phases.title: Germs of translated truncations
phases.description:
Two series have the same germ at an exponent if their coefficients agree from some point to its left through the exponent itself. The exponents with nonzero germ form the closed support, which is well ordered. If any lie above a given cutoff, the first one carries a nonzero scalar germ. The next chapter uses this to make a polynomial relation monic.

Collect all the germs of a series as the coefficients of another generalised power series. When $G$ is Cauchy complete, the convolution formula says that this construction preserves multiplication. At each exponent only finitely many pairs from the two closed supports contribute.
phases.setting: $K$ is a field and $G$ a nontrivial ordered abelian group, with its order topology and the associated group uniformity; $G$ is Cauchy complete if every Cauchy filter on $G$ converges. For $b\in K((G^{\le0}))$ and $\gamma\in G$, $b_{|\gamma}$ is the truncation of $b$ at $\gamma$, the sum of the terms of $b$ with exponent at most $\gamma$, and $b^{|\gamma}=t^{-\gamma}b_{|\gamma}$ is the translated truncation, again an element of $K((G^{\le0}))$ [Ber00, Def. 6.1]. $J$ is the ideal of series whose support is bounded away from $0$, $[b]$ is the class of $b$ in $K((G^{\le0}))/J$, and $K$ is identified with its image there. The germ of $b$ at $\gamma$ is $[b^{|\gamma}]$. The closed support of a series is the closure of its support in $G$.

phases.title: Polynomial presentations
phases.description:
Suppose $G$ is Cauchy complete. Start with a subalgebra $S$ of the ring of germs whose elements have representatives with all their germs in $S$. If $S$ is proper, choose a series with germ outside $S$. Translate the first exponent where its germ lies outside $S$ to $0$ and call the resulting germ $x$. All earlier germs lie in $S$. A polynomial relation on $x$ gives a monic relation of the same degree. Take a monic relation of least degree $d$, with next coefficient $p_{d-1}$. At negative exponents near $0$ the leading term disappears. Minimality forces the next coefficient to vanish there too. The binomial theorem identifies it with the corresponding germ of a representative of $p_{d-1}+dx$, so $p_{d-1}+dx\in K$. In characteristic zero this contradicts $x\notin S$.

Thus adjoining $x$ gives a polynomial extension. Zorn's lemma now presents any subalgebra whose elements have representatives with all their germs in it as a polynomial ring over $K$. Both the full ring of germs and the image of the germs with support of cardinality less than $\kappa$ have this property. For real exponents a series with only constant germs has finite support. Lifting new germs together with their truncations presents $K((\mathbb R^{\le0}))$ as a polynomial ring over its finite-support subring. That subring is a GCD domain [LM24, Fact 2.5.2], so Gauss's lemma gives greatest common divisors in the full series ring.
phases.setting:
$K$ is a field and $G$ a nontrivial ordered abelian group, with its order topology and the associated group uniformity. Write $A=K((G^{\le0}))$ and $Q=A/J$. The germs of $b\in A$ are the classes $[b^{|\xi}]$, $\xi\in G$. For a $K$-subalgebra $S\subseteq Q$, $A(S)$ is the set of series all of whose germs lie in $S$; for $E\subseteq A$, $[E]$ is the image of $E$ in $Q$. A $K$-subalgebra $E\subseteq A$ is closed under truncation if $b_{|\eta}\in E$ for all $b\in E$ and $\eta\in G$. $K(G^{\le0})$ is the subring of series with finite support, and $Y$, $Y_i$ denote polynomial indeterminates.

Hypothesis (H): $G$ is Cauchy complete, $S\subseteq Q$ is a $K$-subalgebra with $S\subseteq[A(S)]$, $X\in A$ satisfies $[X^{|\xi}]\in S$ for all $\xi<0$, and $x=[X]$.

The transcendence lemma and the results that use it assume that $K$ has characteristic $0$, and say so; the other results hold in every characteristic.

phases.title: Reduction along Archimedean classes
phases.description:
This chapter proves that every element of $Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$ is primal under conditions on $G$. Regrouping exponents along a convex subgroup $C$ turns $Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$ into a $D+M$ construction over $D=Z+R((C^{<0}))_\kappa$. So $x$ is primal if its regrouping $\hat x$ and its restriction $\rho_C(x)$ are primal and, in case $\rho_C(x)=0$, $R((C))_\kappa$ is the fraction field of $D$; this step lemma carries the reduction.

The proof is an induction on the order type of the set of nonzero Archimedean classes met by the support. If the set is finite, take $C$ below the leading class; the regrouped series has real exponents, so it is primal by the GCD theorem of Chapter 2. Otherwise take $C$ below a limit of classes. Then the regrouped series is primal because its germ is primal, by the polynomial presentation of the ring of germs, and because restrictions to the convex subgroups $\Gamma_{\preceq q}$ split off factors whose set of classes has smaller order type.
phases.setting:
Vocabulary [LM24, §2.5]: An element $b$ of an integral domain is primal if whenever $b$ divides $cd$ there are $b_1,b_2$ with $b=b_1b_2$, $b_1\mid c$ and $b_2\mid d$. A domain has the refinement property if $bc=de$ implies $b=fg$, $c=hi$, $d=fh$, $e=gi$ for some $f,g,h,i$; it has this property exactly when every element is primal, and it is then called pre-Schreier [Zaf87]. A GCD domain is a domain in which any two elements have a greatest common divisor; GCD domains are pre-Schreier [LM24, Fact 2.5.1].

$G$ is an ordered abelian group, $R$ a field, $Z\subseteq R$ a subring, and $\kappa>\aleph_0$ a cardinal. $R((G))_\kappa$ is the field of series whose support has cardinality less than $\kappa$, and $Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$ its subring of series with support in $G^{\le0}$ and constant coefficient in $Z$. For $x\ne0$, $v(x)=\min\operatorname{supp}(x)$, and $v(0)=0$. For a convex subgroup $C$, $\rho_C(x)$ is the restriction of $x$ to $C$, the sum of the terms of $x$ with exponent in $C$.

$[g]$ is the Archimedean class of $g\in G$. Classes are ordered by magnitude: $[g]\prec[h]$ if $n|g|<|h|$ for all $n\ge1$, so $[0]$ is the least class. A series meets the classes of the exponents in its support. The nonzero classes met by $x$ form a set $\mathcal C(x)$, well ordered by $\succ$ as the image of the well-ordered set $\operatorname{supp}(x)\subseteq G^{\le0}$ under the map $g\mapsto[g]$, which is monotone from $\le$ to $\succeq$ on $G^{\le0}$; $\operatorname{ot}\mathcal C(x)$ is its order type. For a nonzero class $\sigma$, $G_{\prec\sigma}$ and $G_{\preceq\sigma}$ are the convex subgroups of elements of class $\prec\sigma$, respectively $\preceq\sigma$. When $G$ is an ordered vector space over an Archimedean ordered field $F$, $H_\sigma$ is a fixed $F$-linear complement of $G_{\prec\sigma}$ in $G_{\preceq\sigma}$. For a set $T$ of nonzero classes, $G_T=\bigcap_{\sigma\in T}G_{\preceq\sigma}$.

When $G$ is a vector space over a field $F$ and $C$ is a convex $F$-subspace, put $\Gamma=G/C$, $L=R((C))_\kappa$ and $D=Z+R((C^{<0}))_\kappa$. For regular $\kappa$, regrouping exponents along an $F$-linear complement of $C$ sends $x$ to $\hat x\in L((\Gamma^{\le0}))_\kappa$, with constant coefficient $\rho_C(x)$, and identifies $Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$ with $D+L((\Gamma^{<0}))_\kappa$.

Conditions [LM24, Thm. 9.0.1]: (A1)$_\sigma$: $H_\sigma\simeq\mathbb R$ as ordered groups. (A2)$_\sigma$: $\operatorname{cf}(G_{\prec\sigma})\ge\kappa$, or $G_{\prec\sigma}=\{0\}$ and $R=\operatorname{Frac}(Z)$. (A3): $Z$ is pre-Schreier. Further conditions, for a set $T$ of nonzero classes: (B1)$_T$: $\operatorname{cf}(G_T)\ge\kappa$, or $G_T=\{0\}$ and $R=\operatorname{Frac}(Z)$. (B2)$_T$: $G/G_T$ is Cauchy complete for its order topology and group uniformity.

phases.title: Surreal numbers and omnific integers
phases.description:
This chapter checks the conditions of the general theorem for $G=\mathbf{No}$. Conway's construction of a number between two small sets carries the argument.

Each complement $H_\sigma$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb R$. Conway's construction gives the cofinality conditions. It also fills small cuts, and a cut criterion turns this into Cauchy completeness of the quotients $\mathbf{No}/\mathbf{No}_T$.

So every element of $\mathbb Z+\mathbb R((\mathbf{No}^{<0}))_\kappa$ is primal. Conway normal form identifies this ring with the omnific integers. Hence the omnific integers have the refinement property, and every irreducible omnific integer is prime.
phases.setting: Fix a Grothendieck universe and let $\kappa$ be its cardinality, a strongly inaccessible cardinal, in particular regular and uncountable. $\mathbf{No}$ is the field of surreal numbers of birthday less than $\kappa$, and a subset of $\mathbf{No}$ is small if its cardinality is less than $\kappa$. This is the usual way to treat Conway's proper class $\mathbf{No}$ [Con76] as a set: the sets of [Con76] become small subsets, and where [LM24, Prop. 2.4.4] says that a class has cofinality $\mathbf{On}$, here it has cofinality at least $\kappa$. $\mathbf{Oz}\subseteq\mathbf{No}$ is the ring of omnific integers, the numbers $x$ with $x=\{x-1\mid x+1\}$. $\mathbf{No}$ is an ordered $\mathbb R$-vector space, and Archimedean classes, $\mathbf{No}_{\prec\sigma}$, $\mathbf{No}_{\preceq\sigma}$, $H_\sigma$ and $\mathbf{No}_T$ are as in the previous chapter, with $G=\mathbf{No}$.
